title: Computer-Aided Engineering & FEA
summary: Finite element analysis workflow, meshing, boundary conditions, and interpretation of structural, modal, and thermal simulations.

sections.heading: What Is CAE?
sections.content:
**Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE)** uses simulation software to predict how a design behaves before anything is built. The workhorse is **Finite Element Analysis (FEA)**, which splits geometry into small elements and solves the physics equations on each — yielding stresses, deformations, temperatures, and natural frequencies that would otherwise require expensive physical prototypes.

CAE sits between [[cad-computer-aided-design|CAD]] and prototyping in the [[new-product-design|NPD]] workflow: validate the model, then build once.

sections.heading: The FEA Workflow
sections.content:
Every FEA study follows three phases:

1. **Pre-processing** — import geometry, assign materials, define mesh, apply boundary conditions and loads
2. **Solution** — the solver assembles the global stiffness matrix and solves the equilibrium equations
3. **Post-processing** — visualize stress/strain/deformation contours, extract factors of safety, verify convergence

The governing equation of linear static FEA is:

$$[K]\,\{u\} = \{F\}$$

where $[K]$ is the global stiffness matrix, $\{u\}$ the nodal displacement vector, and $\{F\}$ the applied force vector.

sections.heading: Discretization & Mesh Quality
sections.content:
The mesh is where accuracy is won or lost. Key concepts:

- **Element types** — tetrahedra (automatic, good for complex solids), hexahedra (structured, more accurate per node), shells (thin-walled parts), beams (frames)
- **Element size** — smaller elements capture stress gradients better but cost solve time
- **Quality metrics** — aspect ratio, skewness, and Jacobian must stay within solver limits; distorted elements corrupt results
- **Convergence** — refine the mesh and confirm results stabilize; if the stress keeps changing with mesh size, the answer is not converged

Rule of thumb: **refine locally where stress concentrates** (fillets, holes, notches) rather than uniformly, so accuracy is achieved where it matters without exploding solve time.

sections.heading: Boundary Conditions & Loads
sections.content:
Boundary conditions (BCs) anchor the model to reality. Common types:

- **Fixed / pinned supports** — constrain translational and/or rotational DOFs
- **Forces & pressures** — applied loads on faces or nodes
- **Displacement/velocity loads** — prescribed motion
- **Thermal loads** — temperature fields driving expansion, or convection/conduction for thermal analysis

Errors here are the #1 cause of wrong FEA results: an over-constrained model predicts artificially high stiffness; an under-constrained model flies apart. **Always verify**: sum of reactions should balance applied loads, and rigid-body motion must be fully restrained.

sections.heading: Types of Analysis
sections.content:
| Analysis | What it predicts | Typical question |
|---|---|---|
| **Static structural** | Stress, deformation, FOS | Will this bracket survive 5 kN? |
| **Modal** | Natural frequencies & mode shapes | Will this shaft resonate at 3000 RPM? |
| **Thermal** | Temperature distribution & heat flux | How hot will the gearbox housing get? |
| **Fatigue** | Life under cyclic loading | How many cycles before crack initiation? |
| **Buckling** | Critical load for instability | Will this column collapse under compression? |
| **CFD** | Fluid flow, pressure, heat transfer | What pressure drop across the manifold? |

For rotating machinery, check that excitation frequencies stay clear of natural frequencies $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$ by a safe margin (typically ±10-20%).

sections.heading: Interpreting Results Correctly
sections.content:
Post-processing is where simulation earns or loses trust:

- **Von Mises stress** is the standard equivalent stress for ductile metals — compare it against yield strength:

$$\sigma_{vm} = \sqrt{\frac{(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2}{2}}$$

- **Factor of Safety** $FOS = \sigma_{yield} / \sigma_{vm}$ — design for the target FOS, not just "under yield"
- **Stress singularities** — sharp re-entrant corners in FEA produce infinite theoretical stress; the value at the singularity node is mesh-dependent and must be ignored (evaluate at the adjacent element or add the real fillet)
- **Peak stress vs. allowable** — always ask: *is this a real stress or a mesh artifact?*

Cross-check FEA against hand calculations (like [[stress-strain-analysis|Hooke's law]] axial stress) on at least one simple load case before trusting the full model.

sections.heading: Simulation-to-Test Correlation
sections.content:
Simulation is a prediction, not proof. The gold standard is **correlation**: instrument a prototype with strain gauges or accelerometers, measure under the same loads, and confirm the FEA within an acceptable band (typically ±10-15% for linear static).

A calibrated model becomes a powerful tool: once correlated on a known case, design variations can be explored virtually — accelerating the [[new-product-design|NPD]] loop and retiring physical prototypes one-by-one.

keyTakeaways: FEA solves [K]{u} = {F} on a discretized mesh — mesh quality governs result accuracy.
Boundary conditions are the #1 source of wrong answers; check reaction balance before trusting results.
Use Von Mises stress against yield strength for ductile metals; watch for stress singularities at sharp corners.
Run a mesh convergence study — if results change with mesh size, they are not converged.
Correlate simulation against physical tests once; then use the validated model for design exploration.
